skills.name: Data capture: forms, data logging, validation and verification

note.text:
Manual (indirect) data capture: data is collected first (paper forms, questionnaires, interviews), then typed in. A good form has clear questions, boxes for each character, tick boxes where possible and instructions.
Data logging: sensors take readings automatically at regular intervals and store them (weather stations, river levels, hospital monitors).
Validation: the computer checks that data is sensible and allowed (range check, type check, length check, presence check, format check). It cannot prove data is correct.
Verification: checks that data was copied correctly (double entry, or visual check against the original).

sections.heading: Collecting data by hand
sections.text:
Some data must be collected from people: opinions, personal details, survey answers. This is done with forms, questionnaires and interviews, and the data is typed in later (indirect capture).
A good form has clear questions and instructions, a box for each character, tick boxes for choices, and enough space. Good forms mean fewer errors when the data is entered.

sections.heading: Data logging
sections.text:
Data logging uses sensors connected to a logger or computer to take readings automatically at fixed intervals, for example every {10} minutes.
Uses: weather stations, river and flood levels, temperature of vaccine fridges, patients' heart rates.
Readings per hour = {60} ÷ interval in minutes. Every {10} minutes gives {6} an hour and {144} a day.

sections.heading: Checking data
sections.text:
• Validation is done by the computer: is the data sensible? Range check (mark {0}–{20}), type check (a number, not text), length check (exactly {9} digits), presence check (not empty), format check (DD/MM/YYYY).
• Verification checks that data was copied correctly: typing it twice (double entry) or comparing with the original document.
Validation can accept data that is sensible but wrong; verification helps catch those mistakes.

key_words.meaning: automatic check that data is sensible
check that data was entered correctly
automatic recording of sensor readings over time
a set of questions to collect information from people

examples: Mark {25} out of {20}: range check fails
Logger every {30} minutes: {48} readings a day

mistake.wrong: Validation proves the data is correct
mistake.right: Validation only checks the data is sensible
mistake.why: A wrong but sensible value passes validation.

worked_example.problem: A weather station in Garoua logs the temperature every {60 * h / n} minutes. How many readings does it store in {h} hours?
steps: Readings per hour = {60} ÷ {60 * h / n} = {n / h}.

cards.idea: Validation checks data is sensible; verification checks it was copied correctly.
example: Age {250}: rejected by a range check.

cards.idea: Range, type, length, presence and format checks.
example: A phone number must have {9} digits: length check.

cards.idea: Data logging: sensors record readings at set intervals.

check.prompt: A data logger records the level of the river Benue every {m} minutes. How many readings are stored in {d} days?

misconceptions.explain: That is the number of hours. Multiply by readings per hour.

pick.r: An automatic check that data is sensible and allowed
e: Sensible data can still be wrong.

pick.r: Checking that data has been copied or entered correctly
w: Checking that data is within a range
e: That is a validation range check.
pick.y: Double entry or comparing with the original.

pick.q: A pupil's age is entered as 14 instead of 15. Validation accepts it. Why?
pick.r: 14 is a sensible age, so validation cannot tell it is wrong
pick.y: Validation checks sense, not truth: verification catches copying errors.

pick.q: A mark must be between 0 and 20.
e: Presence checks a field is not empty.
pick.y: Limits on the value: range check.

pick.q: The 'surname' box cannot be left empty.
A phone number must contain exactly 9 digits.
e: It is the number of characters that matters.
It is more than just not empty.

pick.q: A date must be written DD/MM/YYYY.
e: The pattern matters, not just the length.

questions.prompt: A data logger records the level of the river Benue every {m} minutes. How many readings are stored in {d} days?

misconceptions.explain: That is the number of hours. Multiply by readings per hour.

pick.q: Which is a feature of a well-designed data capture form?
pick.r: Separate boxes for each character and tick boxes for choices
w: One large box for all the answers
Very small writing to save paper
e: One box makes data hard to read and enter.

pick.q: Why might a researcher use a questionnaire instead of sensors?
pick.r: To collect people's opinions, which sensors cannot measure
pick.y: Opinions and personal information need questions.

pick.q: Why is data logging better than a person taking readings for a week?
pick.r: It works continuously and accurately without breaks
w: It is always cheaper than everything
pick.y: No missed readings, no tired observer.
